about.headline: We are reviving the traditional ways of Old Bharat
about.intro: We believe the wisdom of Old Bharat still holds the secret to wholesome living. Age-old recipes, natural cooking methods and ingredients trusted by generations, made with modern quality standards.

blocks.title: How it started
blocks.body:
Our journey began with a simple belief: good food brings people together. A passion for wholesome, authentic flavours grew into a mission to make food that's nourishing, sustainable and crafted with care.

We work closely with farmer families and suppliers who share our values. Every product balances traditional recipes with modern sensibilities, so every bite is rich in taste and goodness.

blocks.title: A note from our founder
blocks.body: Gaurav has spent over 20 years in health and fitness, and has always been fascinated by the wisdom of ancient Indian sciences. He started Rosier to bring those traditions back to modern kitchens, beginning with milk from indigenous Gir cows.

blocks.title: Sustainability
blocks.body: Our products are minimally processed from consciously sourced ingredients. The healthy choices you make for your body should be healthy for the planet too.

faq.a: Ghee made from the milk of indigenous cows like the Gir, which carries the A2 type of beta-casein protein. Ours is made from curd using the bilona method.
Milk is set into curd overnight, then churned with a wooden churner to separate the butter. That butter is slow cooked into ghee. It takes longer, and we think it tastes better.
Khapli is emmer wheat, an ancient heritage grain. We stone grind it on a chakki so the bran and fibre stay in.

articles.title: Curd, churn, cook: how bilona ghee is made
articles.body:
Most ghee on the shelf is made from cream or butter. Bilona ghee takes the long road.

First, whole milk from Gir cows is boiled, cooled and set into curd overnight. Next morning, the curd is churned with a wooden bilona until the butter (makkhan) separates from the buttermilk.

That butter is then slowly cooked until the moisture leaves and what remains is golden, grainy ghee with a nutty aroma.

It takes a lot more milk and a lot more time. That is exactly why it tastes the way Dadi’s did.

articles.title: Khapli: the ancient wheat making a comeback
articles.body:
Khapli, or emmer wheat, is one of the oldest cultivated grains. It was grown across India long before modern wheat varieties took over.

We stone grind it on a chakki at low speed. The flour stays cooler, and the bran and fibre stay in.

Rotis come out a little darker and nuttier than regular atta. Give it two or three meals, and most families don’t go back.

articles.title: Why stone pressed oil tastes different
articles.body:
Most refined oils are extracted with heat and chemical solvents, then bleached and deodorised.

Stone pressing crushes seeds slowly, at low temperature, with nothing added. The oil keeps its natural colour, aroma and flavour.

That’s why our mustard oil has its signature punch, and our groundnut oil actually smells of groundnuts.
